lessons.title: Digital PR campaigns that earn links and mentions
lessons.body:
### What digital PR is (for link builders)

**Digital PR** means creating and pitching stories that journalists, newsletters, creators and bloggers want to cover — and earning links and brand mentions as a result. It differs from classic PR in its measurement (referring domains, referral traffic, branded search, search and AI visibility) and from classic link building in its currency: **news value**, not favours.

For off-page SEO, digital PR is the tactic that most reliably earns links from high-trust, high-relevance publications — the kind no one can buy legitimately. It also produces the unlinked mentions and expert citations that shape how AI answers describe a brand. (The dedicated course **Digital PR, Brand Mentions & E-E-A-T (digital-pr-and-brand-authority)** covers PR strategy and media relations in depth; this lesson focuses on running campaigns for links.)

### Four campaign types

| Type | How it works | Example (illustrative) |
|---|---|---|
| **Reactive / newsjacking** | Add expert insight or data to a story already in the news, within hours | A payroll firm comments on a budget change the same afternoon |
| **Data-led** | Original survey, analysis of public data or your own anonymised platform data | "Rent-to-income ratios across 12 Karachi neighbourhoods" |
| **Expert-led / thought leadership** | Named experts publish predictions, guides or commentary series | A cybersecurity lead's quarterly scam-trend briefing |
| **Creative / consumer** | A visual, interactive or surprising angle on a topic people already care about | A map of the "most walkable" malls in Dubai based on public data |

### What makes a story newsworthy

Journalists ask: *Is it new? Is it relevant to my readers? Is it surprising, useful or emotionally resonant? Is it credible?* Build campaigns around at least two of those. The classic hooks are **timeliness** (a date, a season, a regulation), **proximity** (your city, your region), **conflict or change**, **human interest** and **authority** (a credible source says something specific).

### Campaign workflow

1. **Ideation** — list 20 angles, then kill most. Test each headline against "would I click this if it weren't about my client?"
2. **Validation** — search news for the topic: has it been covered recently? Is there a gap (region, audience, fresher data)?
3. **Data and assets** — methodology page, 3–5 headline findings, charts with a source line, expert quotes approved by the expert.
4. **Landing page** — a crawlable page on the client's site (not a PDF-only download) with the findings, methodology, charts, embed code and press contact. Link it internally to relevant commercial pages.
5. **Media list** — journalists who covered this beat in the last 3–6 months, segmented by national, regional, trade and local outlets; plus newsletters and creators.
6. **Pitching** — personalised, short, with the headline finding in the subject line; stagger by region and time zone; offer exclusives only when you can honour them.
7. **Follow-up and reactive support** — answer questions quickly; send extra cuts of data for local angles.
8. **Coverage tracking** — log each piece: outlet, URL, linked or not, attribute, target page, message pull-through.

### Press releases, newsrooms and link attributes

Distributing a press release through a wire service is fine for exposure, but links in widely syndicated releases should be `nofollow`; Google lists large-scale press-release links with optimised anchors among link spam patterns. Your value comes from journalists who write their **own** stories. Keep a newsroom page with releases, expert bios, brand assets and a press contact — it makes you easier to cover and cite.

### Ethics and compliance

- Never pay journalists for coverage or links; most outlets forbid it and it breaches their codes.
- Don't invent data, inflate sample sizes or present polls as representative when they aren't.
- Respect embargoes you agree to.
- If you work with creators, disclose paid partnerships under advertising rules (FTC in the US, ASA/CAP in the UK, and local rules in the UAE, KSA and Pakistan) and use `sponsored` on any resulting links.

### Measuring a campaign

| Layer | Metric |
|---|---|
| Coverage | Pieces of coverage; unique referring domains; share linked vs unlinked; share followed vs `nofollow`/`sponsored` |
| Quality | Relevance of outlets (trade, regional, national); message pull-through (did they report the finding correctly?) |
| Outcome | Referral sessions and conversions; branded search impressions in Search Console; change in visibility of the landing page and linked commercial pages vs a baseline |
| Longevity | New links to the landing page in months 2–6 (evergreen data keeps earning) |

### Worked example (illustrative)

A Lahore property portal analyses its own anonymised listings to produce a quarterly rent index for 12 neighbourhoods, with a methodology page and a named data analyst. The first release is pitched to national business desks, Lahore city reporters and two property newsletters; a separate cut for Islamabad goes to Islamabad reporters. Coverage includes several linked articles, more unlinked mentions and a radio interview. The team converts two unlinked mentions via polite requests, adds the index page to the main navigation, and schedules the next quarterly release — each edition refreshes the story and the links.

### Common mistakes

- Pitching a product launch as "news" when it only matters to you.
- Hosting findings only in a PDF or a social post, leaving journalists nothing to link.
- Blasting a generic release to thousands of contacts.
- Measuring only link count and ignoring message accuracy, brand search and referrals.
keyTakeaways: Digital PR earns links and mentions with news value: reactive, data-led, expert-led and creative campaigns.
Every campaign needs a crawlable landing page with findings, methodology, charts and a press contact.
Wire press-release links should be nofollow; value comes from journalists writing their own stories.
Measure coverage, quality, outcomes and longevity — not just link count.

lessons.title: AI-assisted link-building workflows with human QA
lessons.body:
### Where AI genuinely helps

Large language models (LLMs) such as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini are good at **reading and summarising text**, **classifying** pages into categories you define, **extracting** structured fields, and **drafting** from templates and notes. In link building that maps to:

| Task | AI role | Human role |
|---|---|---|
| Prospect triage | Summarise a site's recent topics; classify page type; flag "write for us — all topics" menus | Decide; read two articles for shortlisted sites |
| Personalisation research | Summarise a journalist's last five articles into beats and angles | Choose the angle; write the first line |
| Drafting | Draft the body of a segment template from your notes | Edit, fact-check, send |
| Coverage tracking | Extract outlet, date, whether your brand is linked, and quoted finding from an article | Spot-check accuracy |
| Asset support | Clean data, draft chart captions, translate summaries | Verify every number and quote |

### Where AI must not decide

- **Whether a site is safe to work with.** Link sellers hide their menus; only human review and evidence decide.
- **Facts, findings and quotes.** Models can invent plausible numbers and compliments. Every claim in an email must come from your data or your notes.
- **Volume.** AI makes it cheap to send thousands of "personalised" emails. That is spam with better grammar, and it will damage your sender reputation and your brand.
- **Personal data.** Do not send contacts' personal data to an AI provider unless your organisation's agreements and privacy notice cover it; prefer sending only public page text.

### Hands-on: a prospect-triage pipeline in Python

This script fetches each prospect page, extracts visible text, and asks an LLM to return structured JSON that goes into your sheet as **notes for a human**. It uses the Anthropic Python SDK; the same pattern works with other providers' SDKs. Set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` (a current model ID from the provider's docs) as environment variables — never hard-code keys.

```python
import csv
import json
import os
import sys

import anthropic
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

client = anthropic.Anthropic()                 # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
MODEL = os.environ["ANTHROPIC_MODEL"]          # e.g. set from the current models list

SYSTEM = (
    "You classify web pages for a link-building team. Use ONLY the page text provided. "
    "Return JSON with keys: page_type (one of resource_list, news_article, blog_post, "
    "guest_post_menu, product_page, other), main_topics (list of up to 5 strings), "
    "accepts_paid_posts (true, false or \"unknown\"), evidence (short quotes from the text). "
    "If the text does not show something, use \"unknown\". Do not guess."
)

def page_text(url: str) -> str:
    r = requests.get(url, timeout=15, headers={"User-Agent": "prospect-triage/1.0"})
    r.raise_for_status()
    soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, "html.parser")
    for tag in soup(["script", "style", "nav", "footer"]):
        tag.decompose()
    return " ".join(soup.get_text(" ").split())[:12000]

def classify(url: str) -> dict:
    text = page_text(url)
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model=MODEL,
        max_tokens=600,
        system=SYSTEM,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"URL: {url}\n\nPAGE TEXT:\n{text}"}],
    )
    raw = msg.content[0].text.strip()
    start, end = raw.find("{"), raw.rfind("}")
    return json.loads(raw[start:end + 1])

rows = []
with open("prospects.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        try:
            result = classify(row["url"])
            row["ai_notes"] = json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False)
        except (requests.RequestException, anthropic.APIError, ValueError) as e:
            row["ai_notes"] = f"error: {e}"
            print(f"{row['url']}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        row["human_decision"] = ""               # filled in by a person
        rows.append(row)

with open("prospects_triaged.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(rows[0].keys()))
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(rows)
```

Run it on a small batch first, compare the model's notes with your own judgement on 20 pages, and only then scale. Log the model ID and date with the output so results are reproducible.

### A drafting prompt that forbids invention

```text
You draft outreach emails. Write the BODY ONLY (no greeting, no first line, no signature),
max 90 words, British English, plain text.
Use ONLY these facts: {{facts}}
Segment template: {{template}}
Rules: do not invent statistics, compliments, article titles or claims about the recipient.
If a needed fact is missing, write [MISSING: what] instead.
```

The `[MISSING: …]` convention makes gaps visible instead of letting the model fill them with fiction. A human writes the first line from real research and reads the whole email before it is sent.

### Quality controls that keep AI honest

- **Sampling:** a reviewer checks 10% of AI-classified rows each week; if disagreement exceeds a threshold you set (for example 1 in 10), tighten the prompt or stop using AI for that task.
- **Blocklists win:** a domain on your blocked list is never re-qualified by AI.
- **No auto-send:** AI drafts go to a queue; nothing is sent without a human click.
- **Disclosure where expected:** never present AI-generated text as a named expert's quote.

### Worked example (illustrative)

A small agency in Islamabad qualifies about 150 new prospects a week for three clients. With the triage script, reviewers read AI notes first and open full pages only for plausible candidates. They find that the model reliably spots guest-post menus and topic mixes but occasionally labels news round-ups as resource lists, so they add an example of each to the system prompt. Weekly sampling shows agreement improves; the time saved goes into better first lines and relationship follow-ups rather than more emails.

### Common mistakes

- Letting AI decide which sites are safe.
- Sending AI-drafted emails without a human first line and review.
- Scaling send volume because drafting got cheaper.
- Pasting contacts' personal data into AI tools without the right agreements.
keyTakeaways: Use LLMs to summarise, classify, extract and draft — not to decide which sites are safe or to invent facts.
Structured JSON output with an evidence field makes AI notes easy to review in a sheet.
Forbid invention in prompts and mark missing facts explicitly; a human writes the first line and approves every send.
Sample AI decisions weekly, keep blocklists authoritative, and protect personal data.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the safest role for an LLM in prospect qualification?
options: Producing notes (topics, page type, evidence) for a human reviewer
knowledgeCheck.explanation: LLMs speed up reading; humans make the qualification decision using evidence.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why include '[MISSING: ...]' in a drafting prompt?
options: So gaps are visible instead of being filled with invented facts
It is required by the API
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Explicit gap markers prevent fabricated statistics or compliments from slipping into outreach.

knowledgeCheck.question: Drafting got 10x cheaper with AI. What should happen to send volume?
options: Stay focused on qualified prospects; reinvest time in research and relationships
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Cheap drafting does not change what makes outreach work: relevance and personalisation. More volume harms deliverability and reputation.

lessons.title: Building relationships that compound
lessons.body:
### Why relationships beat transactions

A single link from a pitch is a one-off. A relationship with a journalist, editor, community organiser or complementary business can produce citations, collaborations, referrals and introductions for years. The most effective link builders spend a meaningful share of their time on relationships rather than cold outreach.

### Where relationships come from

- **Successful outreach**: every "yes" is the start of a relationship, not the end of a transaction.
- **Giving first**: sharing a journalist's article, offering data without an ask, introducing two contacts who can help each other.
- **Showing up**: industry events, meetups, conferences, webinars, trade shows (GITEX in Dubai, local chambers of commerce, SEO meetups in Karachi, Lahore, London or New York).
- **Being useful in public**: answering questions in professional communities, publishing helpful posts on LinkedIn, contributing to open resources.

### A lightweight relationship system

Use your CRM or a simple spreadsheet:

```text
Name | Publication/Org | Beat/Topics | How we met | Last contact | What they need |
What we've given | What they've given | Next touch (date + idea)
```

Rules of thumb:

1. **Know their beat.** Read what they publish. Note what topics they cover and what formats they like.
2. **Offer before you ask.** Tip them off to a story that is not about you. Share data they could use.
3. **Be reliable.** When you promise a quote by 3pm, deliver by 2pm. Journalists remember sources who save their deadlines.
4. **Respect boundaries.** No pestering; no pitching everything you do.
5. **Close loops.** Thank them when coverage runs and share it with your audience.

### Relationship-driven tactics

| Tactic | Example |
|---|---|
| Source relationships | A retail journalist asks you first when e-commerce data is needed |
| Content collaborations | Co-authored report with a complementary SaaS company |
| Community partnerships | Sponsoring and speaking at a local startup meetup (sponsor link sponsored; talk recap links earned) |
| Expert panels | Hosting a roundtable and publishing insights, crediting participants |
| Alumni and professional networks | University alumni magazines featuring founders' stories |

### Internal relationships matter too

Link building works best when the whole organisation contributes:

- **Sales and account managers** know which clients might co-publish a case study.
- **Product teams** can produce data or tools.
- **Executives and specialists** provide commentary and speaking.
- **PR and social teams** share contacts and amplification.

Create a simple intake: a form or Slack channel where colleagues flag opportunities (a speaking invite, a partner launch, an interesting dataset).

### Ethical lines in relationships

- Do not offer gifts or payment to journalists in exchange for coverage or links; most publications forbid it and it may breach their codes of conduct and your local laws.
- Disclose commercial relationships where relevant.
- Never ask a friend at a publication to add links that do not serve readers.

### Measuring relationship health

Relationship value is long-term, but you can track leading signs: number of active contacts per beat, inbound requests from journalists, repeat coverage, co-created assets. Review quarterly.

### Worked example

A London-based fintech SEO lead meets a trade journalist at a conference, then shares a useful regulatory analysis without asking for coverage. Months later, the journalist emails asking for comment on a new rule; the lead responds within an hour with a clear, specific quote. Over the next year the journalist cites the company in several articles — some with links, some without — and introduces the lead to a podcast host. (Illustrative scenario.)

### Hands-on: a relationship tracker that nags you (politely)

Turn the tracker into a working tool with a few formulas (Google Sheets):

```text
A Name | B Outlet/Org | C Beat | D Last contact (date) | E Cadence (days) | F Last gave | G Last asked
H Days since contact:   =IF(D2="", "", TODAY()-D2)
I Due?                  =IF(H2="", "new", IF(H2>=E2, "due", ""))
J Give/ask balance:     =IF(AND(F2<>"", G2<>""), IF(F2>=G2, "gave last", "asked last"), "")
```

Add conditional formatting so `due` rows turn amber, and filter weekly on `I = "due"`. The **give/ask balance** column is the honest one: if the last interaction with someone was *you asking*, your next touch should be giving — a tip, a data cut, an introduction, sharing their work.

### Relationships with creators and communities

Relationships are no longer only with journalists. Newsletter writers, YouTubers, podcast hosts, community moderators and subject-matter creators increasingly shape both search results and AI answers (forums and videos are frequently summarised). The same rules apply: know their audience, give first, disclose any commercial relationship (FTC, ASA/CAP and local rules), and mark any paid links `sponsored`.

- Only contacting people when you want something.
- Treating a relationship as a pipeline for links, not a two-way exchange.

lessons.title: Measuring link campaigns
lessons.body:
### Measure what matters to the business

Link reports full of third-party metric jumps satisfy nobody for long. Good measurement connects link activity to outcomes the business cares about, while being honest about attribution.

### A measurement framework in three layers

**1. Output (did we do the work?)**

- Prospects qualified, pitches sent, reply rate, positive reply rate.
- Links and mentions won, by tactic.
- Time or cost per link, by tactic.

**2. Quality (was it the right work?)**

- **New relevant referring domains** — count unique domains, not total links.
- Share of links that are editorial and in-content.
- Relevance mix (industry, local, trade, national media).
- Mentions without links (brand exposure still counts).
- Follow/nofollow/sponsored mix (reported factually; nofollow is not "failure").

**3. Outcome (did it matter?)**

- **Referral traffic** and conversions from linking pages (GA4: Traffic acquisition by session source).
- **Organic performance of target pages**: impressions, clicks and rankings for target queries in Search Console, compared against a baseline and, where possible, against pages that did not receive links.
- **Branded search demand**: branded query impressions in Search Console — often rises after strong coverage.
- **Leads and revenue** attributed to organic and referral channels over time.

### Setting a baseline

Before the campaign, record:

- Referring domains to the target pages and the site (from one consistent tool — do not switch tools mid-campaign).
- Search Console clicks and impressions for target pages and query groups.
- Branded impressions.
- Referral traffic levels.

### A monthly report layout

```text
1. Summary: 3 bullets — what we won, what moved, what's next
2. Wins: table of new links/mentions (publication, page, type, follow status, target URL)
3. Quality: new relevant referring domains by category
4. Outcomes: target-page clicks/impressions vs baseline; referral sessions and conversions;
   branded impressions trend
5. Pipeline: pitches in progress, relationship touchpoints, upcoming assets
6. Learnings: which tactics and angles worked; what we'll change
```

### Attribution honesty

Rankings respond to many factors, often with delays of weeks or months, and links are processed over time. Good practice:

- **Use control groups**: compare pages that received links with similar pages that did not.
- **Annotate confounders**: site changes, algorithm updates, seasonality, PR spikes.
- **Report ranges and trends**, not single-day rank snapshots.
- **Avoid claiming causation** from correlation — say "target pages' non-brand clicks rose X% over the quarter while comparable pages without new links were flat", with numbers from your real data.

### Unit economics

Estimate cost per relevant referring domain by tactic (people time plus tools and asset production). Combined with outcomes, this shows where to invest. For example, an agency might find that unlinked mention reclamation is cheap per link but limited in volume, while a data study is expensive but produces higher-quality links and brand exposure. Your numbers will differ — calculate them.

### Tools

- Search Console Links report (Google's sample of links; not complete, but free and useful).
- One primary third-party backlink index for consistency, plus alerts for new/lost links.
- GA4 for referral traffic and conversions.
- A simple dashboard (Looker Studio or similar) combining these.

### Qualitative wins worth reporting

Not everything valuable fits a chart. Record, with evidence: a journalist who now contacts you first for comment; an invitation to speak or contribute; a partner who proposes a co-marketing project; sales calls where prospects mention seeing your research; and citations of your brand or data in AI-generated answers (spot-checked manually, because measurement there is still immature). These signal growing authority even before search metrics move.

### Lost links

Monitor lost links monthly. Common causes: page deleted, redesign, link removed by editor, or your URL changed. Reclaim where possible (redirect your changed URLs; politely ask about removed links when relevant).

### Hands-on: pull target-page data from the Search Console API

Clicking through the UI is fine for one page; for a campaign with 20 target pages and a control group, use the Search Console API. Create a Google Cloud service account, enable the **Google Search Console API**, and add the service account's email as a user on the property. Then (requires `google-api-python-client`, `google-auth` and `pandas`):

```python
import os
import pandas as pd
from google.oauth2 import service_account
from googleapiclient.discovery import build
from googleapiclient.errors import HttpError

SITE = "sc-domain:example.com"              # or "https://www.example.com/" for URL-prefix
KEY_FILE = os.environ["GSC_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON"]
creds = service_account.Credentials.from_service_account_file(
    KEY_FILE, scopes=["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/webmasters.readonly"])
gsc = build("searchconsole", "v1", credentials=creds)

def page_daily(url: str, start: str, end: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    body = {
        "startDate": start, "endDate": end,
        "dimensions": ["date"],
        "dimensionFilterGroups": [{"filters": [
            {"dimension": "page", "operator": "equals", "expression": url}]}],
        "rowLimit": 25000,
    }
    try:
        rows = gsc.searchanalytics().query(siteUrl=SITE, body=body).execute().get("rows", [])
    except HttpError as e:
        raise SystemExit(f"Search Console API error for {url}: {e}")
    return pd.DataFrame([{"date": r["keys"][0], "clicks": r["clicks"],
                          "impressions": r["impressions"], "page": url} for r in rows])

targets = ["https://www.example.com/services/ecommerce-seo/"]
controls = ["https://www.example.com/services/local-seo/"]
frames = [page_daily(u, "2026-03-01", "2026-08-31").assign(group=g)
          for g, urls in (("target", targets), ("control", controls)) for u in urls]
df = pd.concat(frames)
df["month"] = df["date"].str[:7]
print(df.groupby(["group", "month"])[["clicks", "impressions"]].sum())
```

Compare the **change** in target pages with the change in controls over the same months. Annotate campaign launch dates and known updates. Remember Search Console data is aggregated and some queries are anonymised; trends matter more than single days.

### Cost per relevant referring domain (sheet)

```text
=(Hours * HourlyRate + ToolCosts + AssetCosts) / NewRelevantReferringDomains
```

Calculate it per tactic each quarter. The number is rarely flattering and always useful.

### Branded demand and AI visibility

Add two rows to the outcome layer: branded query impressions (Search Console, filtered with a regex on your brand name and common misspellings) and AI visibility (the Generative AI performance report in Search Console, AI-assistant referrals in GA4, and your monthly prompt panel). Report them as trends with annotations, not as proof of causation.

### Common mistakes

- Reporting only DA/DR changes.
- Counting total links instead of unique relevant referring domains.
- Switching backlink tools mid-campaign and comparing incompatible numbers.
- Promising ranking outcomes by a date.
keyTakeaways: Measure in three layers: output, quality, outcome.
Count unique relevant referring domains and in-content editorial links, not raw link totals or DA/DR changes.
Tie outcomes to target-page performance, referral traffic, branded demand and revenue against a baseline.
Use control groups and annotate confounders for honest attribution.

lessons.title: Competitor backlink analysis
lessons.body:
### What competitor analysis tells you

Competitor backlink analysis answers three questions: **who links in our space**, **what content earns those links**, and **where are the gaps** we can realistically close. It is also a reality check on the link profile needed to compete.

### Choose the right competitors

Your **search competitors** may differ from your business competitors. For a Karachi digital agency, the pages ranking for "technical SEO audit" might include global SaaS blogs, a UK agency and a news publisher. Pick:

- 3–5 sites ranking for your priority query groups (from Search Console and a rank tracker).
- 1–2 direct business competitors of similar size.
- 1 aspirational leader.

### The analysis workflow

**Step 1: Profile overview**

For each competitor, from one tool: referring domains trend (growing, flat, falling), new and lost domains per month, anchor text distribution, follow/nofollow mix, top countries/TLDs of linking sites.

Look for patterns: a sudden spike of referring domains with exact-match anchors may indicate paid links (do not copy it); a steady climb often reflects content and PR.

**Step 2: Top linked pages**

The "best by links" report shows which pages attract links. Classify each:

| Page type | Example | Replicable? |
|---|---|---|
| Data study | "State of e-commerce in the Gulf 2025" | Yes — with our own better or more specific data |
| Free tool | Keyword density checker | Maybe — is there a better angle? |
| Guide | "What is hreflang?" | Yes — if we can be better or more localised |
| Home page | Brand links, directories, partners | Partly — partnerships and mentions |
| Press/news | Funding announcement | No — situational |

**Step 3: Link gap (link intersect)**

Find domains linking to **two or more competitors but not you**. These sites are demonstrably willing to link in your space.

```text
Link intersect: target = ours.example
Competitors: comp-a.example, comp-b.example, comp-c.example
Filter: domains linking to ≥2 competitors, not linking to us
Output columns: domain, linked competitors, linking page, link type, estimated traffic
```

Qualify every result with the link opportunity checklist. Classify by the tactic that could win it: resource page, industry directory (legitimate, curated), media coverage, partner listing, conference sponsor, guest contribution, podcast.

**Step 4: Link types and tactics**

Sample 30–50 competitor links manually. Estimate what share come from: editorial media, resource pages, partners/integrations, events, directories, guest posts, and questionable sources. This reveals their strategy — and what you should *not* imitate.

**Step 5: Anchor and target patterns**

Which pages receive links, and with what anchors? If competitors' commercial pages get links directly, how (partners, directories)? If links flow mainly to content assets, how do they pass value to commercial pages through internal linking?

### Reading the results sensibly

- **Do not chase parity for its own sake.** A competitor's 5,000 referring domains may include many low-value ones. Focus on relevant, reachable, high-quality gaps.
- **Watch for spam footprints** in competitor profiles. Seeing competitors "get away with" paid links is not a reason to follow; the links may already be ignored, and your client bears the risk.
- **Consider content gaps too.** If competitors earn links with data you do not have, the solution may be a new asset, not outreach.

### Worked example (illustrative)

An Abu Dhabi dental clinic compares itself with three competitors ranking in the local pack and organic results. The link intersect shows several relevant opportunities: a community health portal listing clinics, two local parenting blogs that reviewed family dentists, and a university dental faculty page listing training partners. One competitor's profile contains many links from unrelated overseas "guest post" blogs with keyword anchors — noted as a risk, not a tactic. The plan targets the health portal (legitimate listing), a genuinely useful children's dental care guide for the parenting blogs, and a training partnership with the faculty.

### Output

End the analysis with a short, prioritised list:

```text
Opportunity | Tactic | Effort | Expected value | Owner | Target date
```

### Hands-on: a link intersect in pandas

Most backlink tools have a built-in link intersect report. When you need it across tools, for more competitors or combined with your audit sheet, do it yourself from **referring-domain exports** (one CSV per site; adjust the column name to your tool):

```python
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

DOMAIN_COL = "Domain"                       # adjust to your export's column name
ours = "ours.example"
competitors = ["comp-a.example", "comp-b.example", "comp-c.example"]

def domains(site: str) -> set[str]:
    df = pd.read_csv(Path("exports") / f"{site}.csv")
    return set(df[DOMAIN_COL].str.lower().str.removeprefix("www."))

ours_set = domains(ours)
counts: dict[str, list[str]] = {}
for comp in competitors:
    for d in domains(comp) - ours_set:
        counts.setdefault(d, []).append(comp)

gap = (pd.DataFrame([{"domain": d, "links_to": ", ".join(c), "n_competitors": len(c)}
                     for d, c in counts.items()])
         .query("n_competitors >= 2")
         .sort_values("n_competitors", ascending=False))
gap["tactic"] = ""           # resource page, directory, media, partner, event, podcast...
gap["decision"] = ""         # filled in after the quality checklist
gap.to_csv("link_gap.csv", index=False)
print(f"{len(gap)} domains link to 2+ competitors but not to us")
```

Then qualify the output with your link opportunity checklist and assign a tactic to each domain. The raw export is a *list of places to look*, not a to-do list.

### Competitor analysis for AI visibility

Extend the analysis beyond links: for your prompt panel's key questions, note which sources AI answers cite when they mention competitors (review sites, trade media, forums, YouTube). Those sources often overlap with your link gap — and they tell you where your brand is simply absent from the conversation.

### Common mistakes

- Choosing only business competitors, missing the sites that actually rank.
- Copying competitors' spammy link sources.
- Presenting raw link gap exports with thousands of unqualified domains.
keyTakeaways: Pick search competitors that actually rank for your priority queries, not only business rivals.
Analyse profile trends, top linked pages, link intersect gaps, link types and anchor patterns.
Qualify every gap with your quality checklist; never copy spam footprints.
Turn findings into a short prioritised list of opportunities, tactics and owners.

lessons.title: Building a 90-day link plan
lessons.body:
### From ideas to a plan

You now have the ingredients: quality standards, policy knowledge, tactics, outreach skills, measurement and competitor insights. This lesson assembles them into a realistic 90-day plan for a client — the kind of plan an agency can sell, deliver and report on.

### Step 1: Define goals and target pages

- **Business goal**: for example, increase qualified leads from organic search for "SEO services for e-commerce" in the UAE and UK.
- **Target pages**: the service page, two supporting guides, and one linkable asset to build.
- **Baseline**: referring domains, target-page Search Console data, referral traffic, branded impressions.

### Step 2: Audit the starting point

- Current link profile health (any legacy manipulative links? manual actions?).
- Lost links to reclaim (404s with links).
- Unlinked mentions to convert.
- Existing assets with link potential.
- Relationships and partnerships already in place.

### Step 3: Choose a tactic mix

Balance quick wins with compounding work:

| Horizon | Tactics | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Weeks 1–3 | Link reclamation, unlinked mentions, partner listings | Fast, low effort, uses existing equity |
| Weeks 2–8 | Linkable asset creation (e.g. data study or tool); expert commentary programme | Compounding value; builds PR capability |
| Weeks 4–12 | Asset outreach, resource pages, broken-link building, podcast guesting | Scale earned links from the asset |
| Ongoing | Relationship building, internal linking from assets to commercial pages | Makes links count |

### Step 4: Resource and capacity plan

Estimate time honestly. Illustrative weekly capacity for one link specialist: prospecting and qualifying, outreach and follow-up, relationship touches, reporting. Asset creation needs research, writing, design and development time. If the capacity is not there, reduce scope rather than cut quality.

### Step 5: The plan document

```text
90-day link plan — [Client]
Goal: [business goal]; Target pages: [URLs]
Baseline (date): referring domains [n]; target-page clicks [n]; referral sessions [n]
Standards: link quality checklist v2; no paid followed links; disclosure rules apply

Month 1
 - Reclaim links to 404s (redirect map) — owner: tech SEO
 - Convert unlinked mentions from last 12 months — owner: outreach
 - Partner and association listings audit — owner: account manager
 - Asset: plan and field survey (methodology agreed) — owner: research
 - Expert bios live; journalist request monitoring set up — owner: PR
Month 2
 - Publish asset; internal links to service pages
 - Journalist and blogger outreach (segment templates, personalised)
 - Resource page and broken-link prospect lists (qualified)
Month 3
 - Continued outreach and follow-ups; podcast pitches (5 shows)
 - Refresh top guide; pitch to resource pages
 - Quarter review: outputs, quality, outcomes; plan next quarter

Reporting: monthly (template), quarterly review
Risks: asset delays; low reply rates → adjust angle/segments
```

### Step 6: Set expectations

Explain to the client:

- Link building compounds; the first month often produces fewer links than later months.
- Outcomes in search lag behind link acquisition and depend on many factors.
- Some coverage will be nofollow or unlinked — still valuable for brand and traffic.
- You will not buy links or use networks, and why that protects them.

### Step 7: Review and adapt

At the end of each month, compare tactics by cost per relevant referring domain and by outcome contribution. Shift effort towards what works in that niche. Keep a "learnings" log — the most valuable internal asset an agency builds over time.

### Adapting for small budgets

For a small local business with a few hours a month: focus on reclamation, local partnerships, community sponsorships (sponsored links), local media stories, and one useful local resource. For enterprise clients: dedicated research assets, a PR programme, and multi-market outreach teams with local-language pitching (Arabic, Urdu, English).

### 2026 additions to the plan

Add three workstreams that reflect how search now works:

| Workstream | What to do | Measure |
|---|---|---|
| Entity and mentions hygiene | Correct outdated facts in top-cited sources; consistent `Organization` data and profiles | Corrections made; prompt-panel accuracy |
| Digital PR rhythm | One data-led campaign per quarter plus weekly reactive commentary | Coverage, relevant domains, message pull-through |
| AI-assisted operations | Triage and drafting pipelines with human QA and weekly sampling | Hours saved; agreement rate; reply rate unchanged or better |

### A KPI table the client signs off

```text
KPI                                   Baseline   Q target (directional)   Source
New relevant referring domains          —          set from capacity       Tool (one, fixed)
Editorial in-content share              —          ≥ current               Manual review
Target-page clicks vs controls          —          outperform controls     Search Console
Referral sessions → conversions         —          trend up                GA4
Branded query impressions               —          trend up                Search Console
AI visibility (panel + GenAI report)    —          qualitative             Panel, Search Console
```

Agreeing directional targets rather than guaranteed link counts protects quality: nobody is tempted to hit a number with links you would not show a Google reviewer.

### Next steps beyond this course

For AI answer visibility end to end, continue with **AI Search Optimization (ai-search-optimization-geo)**; for crawlability, internal linking and site architecture that make earned links count, see **Technical SEO Mastery (technical-seo-mastery)**; and if your plan includes large page systems, read **Programmatic SEO and AI Content at Scale (programmatic-seo-and-ai-content-at-scale)** before publishing at volume.

### Common mistakes

- Plans that list tactics without owners, capacity or dates.
- Promising a fixed number of high-authority links per month (it incentivises low quality).
- Forgetting internal links from earned-link assets to commercial pages.

scenes.narration: Let's pause and stress test a plan. Here's a line from a real looking proposal: twenty DA fifty plus links per month, guaranteed. What questions should you ask? Where will those links come from? Who decides they're relevant? Are any of them paid? What happens if the only way to hit twenty in a slow month is to buy some? Guarantees like this create exactly the incentive that leads to link spam. A better line: we'll pursue these opportunities, with this capacity, measured by relevant domains, target page outcomes and referrals.

scenes.narration: How should the monthly review actually run? Thirty minutes, same agenda every time. First, outputs versus plan: what shipped, what slipped and why. Fourth, cost per relevant domain by tactic. And fifth, decisions: what to stop, what to double, and what to test next month. Write the decisions in the learnings log. After two or three quarters, that log becomes your most valuable asset.

A mention alert search finds three unlinked mentions from gift guides. Then capacity. They have about eight hours a month from me, so I plan realistically: weeks one to three, reclaim and convert mentions; weeks two to eight, build a leather care calculator for how often to condition different leathers; weeks four to twelve, pitch it to gift guides and craft blogs. pool.question: Which is NOT a documented role of links for search engines?
options: Understanding relevance through anchor text and context
Directly setting a page's Core Web Vitals score
pool.explanation: Links aid discovery, relevance and importance; they have nothing to do with CWV.

pool.question: A client wants to 'get DA to 50 this year'. What is the best response?
options: Explain DA is a third-party estimate and reframe goals around relevant links and business outcomes
Agree and buy links to hit it
pool.explanation: Vendor metrics are proxies; goals should be relevant links, visibility and revenue.

pool.question: Which factors generally increase the value of a link? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Being one of 400 sitewide footer links
Topical relevance of the linking page
The linking page being well linked and read
pool.explanation: Relevance, editorial context and the linking page's own signals increase value; sitewide footers do not.

pool.question: Which anchor text profile looks most natural?
options: A mix of brand names, URLs, generic phrases and descriptive topical phrases
pool.explanation: Natural profiles are varied and brand-heavy.

pool.question: Two opportunities: a niche trade journal with modest third-party metrics but real readers in your industry, and a general 'news' site with high metrics that sells posts on any topic. Which is the better target and why?
options: The general site, because metrics are higher
The trade journal, because relevance, editorial standards and real audience outweigh inflated metrics
pool.explanation: Metrics can be manipulated; relevance and editorial integrity predict value and safety.

pool.question: What should you check to see if a prospective linking site is actually indexed?
options: A site: search and a search for a unique sentence from a recent article
pool.explanation: Search operators show whether Google indexes the site's pages.

pool.question: Which statement about links is accurate?
options: Google no longer uses links at all
Links can make any page rank regardless of content
Links help but cannot rescue a page that fails search intent or is noindexed
pool.explanation: Links are one signal among many and cannot override intent mismatch or technical blocks.

pool.question: What attribute should an affiliate link carry?
pool.explanation: Affiliate and paid links should use sponsored (nofollow is also acceptable).

pool.question: Which activities fall under Google's link spam examples? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Earning a citation for original research
Widely distributed keyword-rich links in widget embeds
Sending free products in exchange for reviews with followed links
pool.explanation: Product-for-link swaps, widget links and excessive exchanges are listed; earned citations are not spam.

pool.question: When does Google recommend using the disavow tool?
options: When you have many unnatural links (often ones you built) that have caused or may cause a manual action
Whenever a tool shows toxic links
pool.explanation: Google says most sites don't need it; it's for significant unnatural link problems.

pool.question: Which disavow file lines are correctly formatted? (Choose all that apply.)
pool.explanation: Valid lines are domain: entries, full URLs and # comments.

pool.question: A site receives a manual action for unnatural links. What must precede the reconsideration request?
options: Auditing links, attempting removals, disavowing what remains and stopping the cause
pool.explanation: Reviewers expect genuine, documented clean-up and prevention.

pool.question: A publisher hosts third-party 'best loans' reviews produced by an outside company to benefit from the publisher's ranking strength. The publisher edits them lightly. What applies?
options: Site reputation abuse can still apply, as Google clarified first-party involvement doesn't exempt such content
No policy, because the publisher is involved
pool.explanation: Google clarified that host involvement does not exempt content hosted mainly to exploit the host's signals.

pool.question: How does Google treat rel=nofollow today?
options: As a strict block on crawling
pool.explanation: Nofollow, sponsored and ugc are hints.

pool.question: What is broken-link building?
options: Finding links to dead resources and suggesting a genuinely equivalent replacement
pool.explanation: It helps site owners fix dead links while earning an editorial link.

pool.question: Which assets typically earn links from university resource pages? (Choose all that apply.)
options: A sales page for paid services
pool.explanation: Educational resources get listed; commercial sales pages rarely do.

pool.question: A journalist mentions your study without linking. Best approach?
options: Thank them and politely ask if they'd link the study so readers can see the methodology
pool.explanation: Unlinked mention outreach is polite, reader-focused and fast.

pool.question: You plan a survey-based study. Which practices increase its chances of earning credible links? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Headlines that overstate findings to attract journalists
pool.explanation: Transparency, usability and compliance build credibility; overstated findings damage trust.

pool.question: What is often the quickest link win for an established site?
options: Reclaiming links pointing to your 404 URLs with relevant redirects
pool.explanation: Reclamation restores existing link value quickly.

pool.question: Which partnership linking practice is compliant and natural?
options: A technology partner's integration directory listing your integration
Adding keyword-anchored footer credits across hundreds of client sites
Paying for followed links on partner blogs
Agreeing to link swaps with 50 unrelated sites
pool.explanation: Integration directories reflect real relationships and help users.

pool.question: What makes a podcast pitch effective?
options: A generic request to be a guest
Tailored episode ideas for that show's audience, a short bio and evidence of speaking ability
pool.explanation: Hosts want relevant, valuable episodes.

pool.question: Which element should every prospect row include before outreach?
pool.explanation: Without a hook, the pitch is likely generic and a poor fit.

pool.question: Which outreach behaviours are appropriate? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Verifying email addresses to avoid bounces
Sending from a real person's address with a full signature
pool.explanation: Honesty and list hygiene protect recipients and your sender reputation; fake replies are deceptive.

pool.question: Under UK GDPR, what is commonly relied upon as the lawful basis for relevant B2B outreach to named individuals at companies?
options: Legitimate interests, with a balancing test and transparency
pool.explanation: Legitimate interests is typically used for relevant B2B outreach, with obligations to be transparent and honour objections. (General information, not legal advice.)

pool.question: What is a reasonable length for a cold outreach email?
pool.explanation: Short, specific emails are read and answered more often.

pool.question: A pitch gets no reply after two follow-ups. The prospect is highly relevant. Best next step?
options: Stop this sequence; consider a genuinely different, useful touchpoint months later or build the relationship elsewhere
pool.explanation: Respect silence; relationships can be built in other ways over time.

pool.question: What is the main purpose of the first line of an outreach email?
options: To show specific relevance to the recipient's work
pool.explanation: Specific relevance earns attention.

pool.question: Why avoid attachments in cold outreach?
options: They trigger spam filters and security concerns; links are safer
pool.explanation: Links avoid security and deliverability problems.

pool.question: Which is an outcome metric (not an output metric) for a link campaign?
pool.explanation: Outcomes are business results; outputs are activity.

pool.question: Which approaches support honest attribution of link-building results? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Claiming every ranking gain as caused by links
Comparing target pages with similar pages that did not receive links
Reporting trends rather than single-day snapshots
pool.explanation: Controls, annotations and trends are honest; blanket causal claims are not.

pool.question: Which is the better way to count link-building quality?
pool.explanation: Unique relevant domains reflect breadth of editorial endorsement.

pool.question: What is the most effective way to start a relationship with a journalist?
options: Offer genuinely useful help without an immediate ask
pool.explanation: Giving first builds trust.

pool.question: A report shows a data study earned many links, but target service pages saw no change. What is the most useful next step?
options: Check internal links from the study to service pages and allow time, comparing with control pages
pool.explanation: Internal linking passes value onward; outcomes lag, so measure against controls over time.

pool.question: Why track branded search impressions after a PR-driven link campaign?
options: Coverage often increases brand awareness, reflected in branded searches
pool.explanation: Brand demand is a meaningful effect of coverage.

pool.question: Which practice is unethical when working with journalists?
options: Offering payment or gifts in exchange for links or coverage
pool.explanation: Paying for coverage breaches journalistic codes and link policies.

pool.question: Which competitors should a backlink analysis focus on?
options: Sites that actually rank for your priority queries plus a few direct business rivals
Only the biggest brand in the country
pool.explanation: Search competitors reveal what it takes to rank for your queries.

pool.question: What does a competitor's 'best by links' report primarily reveal?
options: Which pages and asset types attract links in your space
pool.explanation: Top linked pages show link-earning content types.

pool.question: A link gap export returns 3,000 domains. What should you present to the client? (Choose all that apply.)
options: The raw 3,000-row export as the plan
A qualified, prioritised shortlist with tactic, effort and owner
Notes on spam footprints you will not imitate
pool.explanation: Raw exports are not plans; qualify, group and prioritise.

pool.question: In a 90-day plan, why pair linkable assets with internal links to commercial pages?
options: Internal links pass value earned by assets on to pages that convert
pool.explanation: Internal linking helps asset equity support commercial targets.

pool.question: Which is typically a quick win in the first weeks of a link plan?
options: Converting unlinked mentions and reclaiming lost links
pool.explanation: They use existing equity and relationships.

pool.question: What should a 90-day link plan include to be deliverable? (Choose all that apply.)
options: A baseline of links and target-page performance
Owners and dates for each activity
pool.explanation: Plans need ownership, baselines and standards; ranking guarantees are not credible.

pool.question: A competitor spiked by thousands of referring domains in one month with exact-match anchors from unrelated sites. What is the best interpretation?
options: A technical error in your tool only
A successful PR campaign to copy
Proof that link spam works permanently
Likely manipulative links that may be ignored or risky; not a tactic to imitate
pool.explanation: Sudden unnatural spikes with exact anchors are classic manipulation footprints.

pool.question: A client asks you to 'get us into AI Overviews' and suggests buying placements on 200 low-traffic blogs that mention the brand. What does Google's guidance indicate?
options: It is the recommended AEO tactic
Inauthentic mentions are not helpful, and attempts to manipulate generative AI responses fall under spam policies
Mentions are ignored entirely by all systems
It is fine if the blogs use nofollow
pool.explanation: Google's May 2026 guidance calls out inauthentic mentions, and its spam policies now explicitly include manipulation of AI responses in Search. Earned coverage is the sustainable route.

pool.question: According to Google, what is the relationship between AI Overviews/AI Mode and core Search systems?
options: They use a completely separate index
They are built on the same crawling, indexing and ranking foundations as Search
pool.explanation: Google's guide says generative AI features build on Search's foundations; good SEO and earned trust signals apply to both.

pool.question: Which TWO measurement approaches give the most reliable view of a brand's AI search visibility today?
options: Search Console (including the Generative AI performance report) and a GA4 channel group for AI-assistant referrals
A fixed monthly prompt panel of real buyer questions, recorded with dates and sources
A single screenshot of one assistant's answer
pool.explanation: First-party data (Search Console, GA4) plus a consistent, dated prompt panel give trends; single screenshots and vendor scores are not reliable measures.

pool.question: In a link audit sheet, a domain gets two automatic flags: 'money anchor' and 'sitewide'. What is the correct next step?
options: Review it manually, record evidence and then classify it
Ignore flags; only tool toxicity scores matter
pool.explanation: Flags prompt review; classification needs human judgement and evidence (for example invoices or identical paid posts).

pool.question: A US news site hosts a third-party 'best payday loans' section that exploits its ranking signals. After Google's August 2026 change, how is site reputation abuse enforced?
options: Outside the EEA a manual action can affect the violating section; inside the EEA Google may separate the section so it ranks on its own merits
Only the whole domain can be penalised, everywhere
Enforcement only happens in the EEA
pool.explanation: Google adjusted enforcement in the EEA after discussions with the European Commission; the policy itself still applies globally.

pool.question: Why should you merge new disavow entries into a master file before uploading?
options: A new upload replaces the previous file for the property
It makes the file load faster
pool.explanation: Because each upload replaces the previous file, forgetting old entries silently un-disavows them.

pool.question: Which campaign landing page setup best supports earning links from coverage?
options: Findings only in a PDF emailed to journalists
A crawlable page with findings, methodology, downloadable charts, a press contact and internal links to relevant commercial pages
A wire release with dofollow links
pool.explanation: Journalists need a citable page; internal links then pass value to commercial pages.

pool.question: A plumber sends local reporters three specific frozen-pipe tips within hours of a cold-snap forecast. Which campaign type is this?
pool.explanation: Adding timely expert insight to a developing story is reactive PR.

pool.question: Your team builds an LLM pipeline that classifies prospect pages. Which TWO controls should be in place?
options: A human makes the qualification decision; AI output is stored as notes with evidence
Weekly sampling of AI classifications against human judgement
Automatic sending of AI-drafted emails to every classified site
Sending contacts' personal data to the model by default
pool.explanation: AI notes speed up review, humans decide, and sampling catches drift. Auto-sending and sharing personal data without agreements are risks.

pool.question: An AI-drafted pitch says 'I loved your recent article on Gulf logistics' but nobody on the team read it. What is the core problem?
options: It is an invented claim about the recipient; prompts must forbid invention and a human must write the first line from real research
pool.explanation: Fabricated compliments are misrepresentation, erode trust and are easy for editors to spot.

pool.question: Since 2024, which requirements do Gmail and Yahoo place on senders that also matter for outreach programmes?
options: No requirements for small senders at all
Authentication (SPF/DKIM), and for bulk senders DMARC, easy unsubscribe and low complaint rates
pool.explanation: Authentication applies to all senders; bulk senders also need DMARC, one-click unsubscribe for marketing mail and low spam complaint rates.

pool.question: Target pages that earned links rose 18% in clicks over a quarter; comparable control pages rose 15%; a core update rolled out mid-quarter. What is the most accurate report statement?
options: Target pages outperformed controls by about three points in a quarter that included a core update; the effect is modest and not proven causal
pool.explanation: Honest attribution compares against controls and annotates confounders rather than claiming causation. (Figures illustrative.)
